title: CSR in India: The Complete Guide for CSR Heads and Teams
excerpt: What Section 135 actually requires, from applicability and the 2% calculation to unspent funds, reporting, and where compliance-only CSR falls short.
content:
Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires companies above set net worth, turnover, or profit thresholds to spend at least 2% of their average net profit on CSR every year, form a CSR Committee, and publicly report what they spent it on. Non-compliance carries financial penalties for both the company and its officers, not just a warning letter.

That’s the rule in one paragraph. Everything below is what it actually means to run CSR under it, year to year, from figuring out whether you’re covered to deciding what to do with the budget once you know you are.

India was the first country in the world to make corporate social responsibility a legal obligation rather than a voluntary gesture. Section 135 came into force with the Companies Act, 2013, was operationalized through the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014, and was substantially tightened by amendments in 2021 that added mandatory implementing-agency registration, defined penalties for the first time, and introduced impact assessment for the largest spenders. If your company has been through a few budget cycles under this law, you’ve likely felt each of those tightening moments as a new form to file or a new deadline to track. This guide covers the law as it stands today, plus where it’s likely headed next.

Who actually has to comply

CSR under Section 135 applies to any company registered in India, private limited, public limited, one-person company, Section 8 company, or a foreign company with a branch or project office here, that crosses any one of three thresholds in the immediately preceding financial year:

  • Net worth above ₹500 crore, or
  • Turnover above ₹1,000 crore, or
  • Net profit above ₹5 crore

Only one threshold needs to be crossed, not all three. A company can have modest turnover and still fall under CSR purely on net profit. The assessment happens every financial year, so a company that qualifies in FY 2025-26 complies with CSR obligations in FY 2026-27, and a company that drops below all three thresholds the following year is no longer obligated, though most companies that qualify once tend to stay above the line.

There’s amendment activity in Parliament around these thresholds right now, with different proposals in circulation about whether they should move up or down. Nothing has been passed and notified as of this writing, so the ₹500 crore / ₹1,000 crore / ₹5 crore figures above are the operative ones. This is worth checking against the current MCA notifications before you finalize a year’s budget, since it’s one of the few numbers in this whole framework that’s actually in motion.

(For the full applicability picture, including how the amendment proposals differ and what each would mean for mid-sized companies, see the companion article: Is Your Company Covered by CSR? Section 135 Applicability, Explained.)

Setting up the CSR Committee

Once a company qualifies, its Board has to constitute a CSR Committee before anything else happens. The committee needs at least three directors, and at least one of them has to be an independent director. It’s this committee, not the Board at large, that formulates the CSR policy, recommends the annual action plan, and monitors spend through the year, with the full Board retaining final approval authority.

For companies where three directors including an independent one isn’t feasible, such as private companies with fewer board members, the rules provide for a smaller committee structure, but the requirement to have a dedicated CSR governance body, rather than folding it into general board business, doesn’t go away.

How the 2% is actually calculated

The obligation is 2% of average net profit over the three immediately preceding financial years, not the current year’s profit and not net profit as your tax filings define it.

That second point trips up more finance teams than anything else in this framework. CSR net profit is computed under Section 198 of the Companies Act, which has different add-backs and exclusions than net profit under the Income Tax Act. Using the tax-return figure instead of the Section 198 figure is the single most common calculation error companies make, and it tends to produce an under-spend that only surfaces at audit time.

For a company in only its first or second year of operation, the average is computed on however many financial years actually exist yet, not backfilled with assumptions.

A simplified version of the math: if a company’s Section 198 net profit was ₹80 crore, ₹95 crore, and ₹110 crore in the three preceding financial years, the average is ₹95 crore, and the CSR obligation for the current year is 2% of that, ₹1.9 crore. That figure, not the current year’s profit, whatever it turns out to be, is the number the CSR Committee plans against.

(Full worked example and the specific add-backs to watch for: How to Calculate Your Company’s 2% CSR Obligation.)

What actually counts as CSR spend

Not every good deed qualifies. Eligible activities have to fall within Schedule VII of the Companies Act, a defined list that covers areas like education, healthcare, poverty and hunger, environmental sustainability, gender equality and women’s empowerment, disaster relief, protection of national heritage and culture, support for armed forces veterans, and promotion of sports at the grassroots and national level, among others. A company’s CSR policy has to map its planned activities to this list, and the Board is responsible for confirming that mapping before spend happens, not after.

Just as important as what’s included is what’s explicitly excluded. Under Rule 2(1)(d) of the CSR Policy Rules, six categories of activity don’t count as CSR no matter how socially beneficial they look on paper:

  • Activities carried out in the normal course of the company’s own business
  • Activities undertaken outside India, with a narrow exception for training Indian sports personnel representing a state, union territory, or the country
  • Any contribution, direct or indirect, to a political party
  • Activities that benefit only the company’s own employees and their families
  • Sponsorship activities undertaken mainly to generate marketing benefit for the company’s products or services
  • Spend that fulfills an obligation the company already owes under a different law, such as labour or land-acquisition legislation

That fourth exclusion catches out more companies than the others. A wellness camp or scholarship program designed for the community at large still qualifies even if some employees’ children happen to benefit, but a program designed exclusively for staff and their families doesn’t count as CSR at all, however genuinely useful it is. The line the MCA draws is about who the activity is designed for, not who incidentally benefits.

There’s a related nuance worth flagging directly, since it comes up constantly in employee-engagement conversations: employee volunteer hours themselves cannot be monetized and counted toward the 2% obligation. You can’t calculate a rupee value for staff time and book it as CSR spend. What you can do is have employees participate in a project that is already CSR-eligible on its own merits, funded through the actual CSR budget. The volunteering adds engagement value on top of the spend; it isn’t a substitute for it.

CSR expenditure also can’t be claimed as a business expense for tax purposes, a rule that’s been in place since the Finance Act, 2014, and it has to be purely monetary and traceable, donations of a company’s own unsold product inventory don’t qualify as CSR spend either.

A related, often-missed rule: administrative overhead for running your CSR program is capped at 5% of total CSR expenditure. Anything you spend on program staff, monitoring visits, or internal coordination beyond that cap doesn’t count toward your 2% obligation, it comes out of the company’s own pocket instead.

Spending it yourself, or through a partner

Companies can run CSR activities directly, but most route funds through an implementing partner, an NGO, trust, or Section 8 company that actually delivers the work on the ground. If you go that route, the partner has to hold CSR-1 registration on the MCA portal. This isn’t optional paperwork: routing funds through an unregistered partner, an international organization without CSR-1 status, or a foreign parent’s foundation gets that expenditure disqualified entirely, meaning it’s treated as unspent regardless of what actually happened on the ground.

Beyond CSR-1, most credible implementing partners also carry provisional or full 12A and 80G registration under the Income Tax Act, which is a separate but related signal of legitimacy worth checking.

In practice: what a well-chosen partnership actually looks like isn’t just a compliance checkbox, it’s a design decision with real range in it. When Sooper Dooper Kids partnered on Dharavi Dreams, a hip-hop theatre production with thirteen teenage performers from Dharavi, the brand’s contribution wasn’t a check written and forgotten. They funded custom stage T-shirts for the performers, and backed a production crew to shoot a music video of the show, a deliberate choice that turned one evening into something that kept reaching people afterward. Neither piece was required by law. Both were the difference between a CSR line item and something the dancers, and eventually 500,000 viewers, actually remembered.

One more distinction worth knowing: international organizations and foreign foundations generally cannot act as the implementing agency for a CSR project. They can be engaged for specific supporting roles, designing a project, monitoring and evaluating it, or building internal capacity among the company’s own CSR staff, but they can’t be the entity actually receiving and deploying the funds on the ground. That role has to sit with a CSR-1 registered Indian entity.

(How to actually vet a partner beyond registration status: Choosing a CSR Implementing Partner: What CSR-1 Registration Actually Means.)

What happens if you don’t spend it all

Underspending isn’t itself illegal, but leaving the money unaddressed is. If CSR spend falls short of the 2% obligation, the company has to account for the gap and move the unspent amount within a defined window, and which window depends on what the money was earmarked for:

  • If the shortfall relates to an ongoing project, the unspent amount goes into a dedicated Unspent CSR Account within 30 days of the financial year’s end, and has to actually be spent within three years or transferred onward. An “ongoing project” for this purpose has a defined ceiling of its own: it can run for a maximum of four years including the year it was approved, or three years counted from the year after commencement, whichever framing you use. A multi-year commitment that runs longer than that stops qualifying as ongoing and needs to be restructured or closed out.
  • If it relates to a non-ongoing commitment, the unspent amount goes to a Schedule VII fund, the PM National Relief Fund or PM CARES among them, within six months of the financial year’s end.

Miss either window and the penalty structure is the same either way: twice the unspent or untransferred amount, or ₹1 crore, whichever is lower, on the company, plus a personal penalty on responsible officers of one-tenth the unspent amount or ₹2 lakh, whichever is lower. Companies that spent the money correctly but simply missed the transfer deadline have been penalized under this rule, so the deadline matters as much as the spend itself.

(Full breakdown of both pathways, with worked numbers: What Happens to Unspent CSR Funds.)

Two deadlines that get confused with each other

A specific, recurring point of confusion: the unspent-fund transfer deadlines above are anchored to the financial year end, while the CSR-2 filing deadline below is anchored to the AGM date. These are not the same clock. A company whose AGM happens well after the financial year closes still has to hit the 30-day or six-month transfer windows on schedule, regardless of when its AGM eventually takes place. Treating both as one deadline, or assuming the later AGM-linked date gives extra room on fund transfers, is a mistake that shows up in compliance reviews more often than it should.

Reporting: what gets filed, and when

CSR compliance doesn’t end when the money moves. Every company under Section 135 has to file Form CSR-2 as an addendum to Form AOC-4, within 30 days of the AGM, digitally signed by the Company Secretary and a director, and certified by a practicing Chartered Accountant. It has to state the CSR obligation amount, actual spend, project-by-project detail, any amount sitting in the Unspent CSR Account, and the reasons for any shortfall.

Alongside that, the company’s Board Report needs its own CSR annexure covering the CSR policy, the CSR Committee’s composition, and the same spend figures, and the CSR policy itself has to be published on the company’s website. Listed companies carry one more layer on top: BRSR (Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting) filings with SEBI, which overlap with but don’t replace the CSR-specific filings.

(What actually gets checked in each filing, and the mistakes that trigger a second look: CSR Reporting and Filing: CSR-2, the Board Report, and What Gets Checked.)

The mistakes that come up most often

Across every stage above, a handful of errors account for most of the compliance problems companies actually run into:

  • Using tax-return net profit instead of Section 198 net profit when calculating the 2% obligation, which almost always produces the wrong number.
  • Routing funds through a partner without confirming CSR-1 registration, which gets the entire expenditure disqualified after the fact, not just flagged.
  • Missing the transfer deadline for unspent funds, even when the underlying spend itself was handled correctly. The penalty applies to the missed deadline, not just to money that was never spent.
  • Booking employee-only welfare programs as CSR, which fails the very first test of what Schedule VII activities are actually for.
  • Treating volunteer hours as a form of CSR expenditure, which isn’t permitted under any reading of the rules, however well-intentioned.

Most of these are avoidable with a compliance calendar and a habit of checking partner registration status before funds move, not after.

Impact assessment: when it’s actually mandatory

Not every company has to formally assess the impact of its CSR work, and not every project within a company that does. The rule (Rule 8(3) of the Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, as amended in 2021) kicks in only when both of these are true: the company’s average CSR obligation over the preceding three years is ₹10 crore or more, and the specific project being assessed has an outlay of ₹1 crore or more and was completed at least a year before the assessment starts.

A company well above the ₹10 crore threshold with only smaller individual projects isn’t required to run a formal assessment, though it’s generally good practice to do one anyway. Where it is mandatory, the assessment has to be done by an independent third-party agency, not in-house, and the cost is capped at 5% of total CSR spend or ₹50 lakh, whichever is lower, a separate cap from the administrative overhead limit mentioned earlier.

Where compliance ends and something better begins

Everything above this line is what the law requires. None of it requires the CSR day itself to feel like anything in particular to the employees showing up to it.

That’s a real gap, and not just an emotional one. According to the National CSR Portal, Indian companies spent roughly ₹34,900 crore across nearly 60,000 projects in FY 2023-24 alone, spread across 14 development sectors. Individual large spenders routinely put hundreds of crores behind single-year programs reaching hundreds of thousands of people, the kind of scale where a company’s CSR choices are shaping entire districts, not just writing a check. At that scale, the difference between a CSR activity employees quietly tolerate and one they actually talk about afterward isn’t a compliance question at all, it’s a design one: whether anyone deliberately built a moment worth remembering into the day, on top of the impact the spend was already required to create.

The law asks a company to prove where the money went. It says nothing about whether the day was worth remembering. That second question is a choice every CSR team still has to make on its own, year after year, project after project, regardless of what Schedule VII allows.

(What the evidence actually says about that gap: Employee Engagement vs. Compliance-Only CSR: What Actually Moves the Needle.)

title: Is Your Company Covered by CSR? Section 135 Applicability, Explained
excerpt: The three thresholds, the edge cases that trip companies up, and what's actually in motion in Parliament right now.
content:
A company falls under Section 135 if, in the immediately preceding financial year, it crossed any one of three thresholds: net worth above ₹500 crore, turnover above ₹1,000 crore, or net profit above ₹5 crore. Only one threshold needs to be crossed, applicability is reassessed every single year, and it’s checked on a standalone basis, one company at a time, even inside a larger group.

That covers the headline rule. The parts that actually trip companies up are the edge cases: group structures, foreign entities, new incorporations, and what happens the year after you first qualify. This article works through each of them.

The three thresholds, one at a time

  • Net worth above ₹500 crore. Calculated from the company’s own balance sheet, not the group’s.
  • Turnover above ₹1,000 crore. Total income from operations for the year, again at the standalone company level.
  • Net profit above ₹5 crore. Computed under Section 198 of the Companies Act, which is a different figure from taxable profit under the Income Tax Act, and excludes things like capital receipts and set-offs of past losses.

Any one of the three is enough. A company with modest turnover but a strong profit margin can still be pulled into CSR purely on the net-profit test, and a capital-intensive company with a large balance sheet can qualify purely on net worth even in a thin-margin year.

A worked example. Say a mid-sized manufacturing company had a net worth of ₹340 crore, turnover of ₹1,150 crore, and net profit of ₹6.2 crore in FY 2025-26. It fails the net worth test and passes both the turnover test and the net profit test. Since only one threshold has to be crossed, this company is squarely covered by Section 135 for FY 2026-27, and its finance team needs to be planning a CSR budget and constituting a CSR Committee well before that year begins, not scrambling once the financial year is already underway.

Applicability resets every year, based on last year’s numbers only

This is the detail most CSR teams get wrong, so it’s worth stating plainly: applicability is not a rolling average and not a permanent status once triggered. It’s checked fresh each year, using only the immediately preceding financial year’s figures. If a company crosses a threshold in FY 2025-26, CSR provisions apply to it for FY 2026-27, evaluated purely on that one year’s numbers, not a multi-year trend.

That cuts both ways. A company that crosses a threshold once and then genuinely falls back below all three the following year is not obligated the year after that, though in practice, few companies large enough to cross these thresholds fall back below them for long.

Holding companies, subsidiaries, and group structures

CSR applicability is assessed on a standalone basis, company by company, not on a consolidated group basis. A holding company being covered by Section 135 does not automatically pull its subsidiaries in, and a subsidiary being covered does not automatically pull in its parent. Each entity in a group has to independently cross a threshold on its own financials before CSR applies to it specifically.

This surprises finance teams at large conglomerates more than anyone else. A profitable subsidiary can be squarely inside CSR while its loss-making parent sits outside it entirely, and the reverse is just as common. The one place group structure does matter: a foreign holding company can fund CSR activity delivered through its Indian subsidiary, and that spend can count toward the subsidiary’s own obligation, provided the subsidiary is the one legally required to spend it under Section 135.

Section 8 companies, the not-for-profit company structure under the Act, are covered by Section 135 exactly the same way any other company is. Being a Section 8 company doesn’t create an exemption.

Foreign companies with an Indian presence

A foreign company, as defined under the Act, is covered if it has a branch office or project office in India and crosses any of the same three thresholds. The relevant net worth, turnover, and net profit figures are computed from the balance sheet and profit and loss account that the foreign company is required to prepare for its Indian operations, not its global consolidated financials. This means a large multinational with a modest Indian branch presence may sit entirely outside Section 135, while the same company’s larger, separately incorporated Indian subsidiary could be squarely inside it, evaluated on its own numbers.

This distinction matters more than it sounds like it should for foreign investors setting up in India. A branch or project office and a locally incorporated subsidiary are treated completely differently for CSR purposes, and the choice of structure, made early, well before anyone is thinking about CSR, ends up determining whether and how these obligations apply years later.

There’s also a practical governance point worth knowing for foreign companies that are covered: the CSR Committee requirement is adjusted for them. Instead of the standard three-director structure, a foreign company’s CSR Committee needs just two people, one of whom has to be a person resident in India, authorized to accept notices and documents on the company’s behalf, and the other nominated by the foreign company itself.

Newly incorporated companies

A company that hasn’t completed three full financial years since incorporation still has its CSR obligation calculated as an average, just over however many years actually exist. A company in only its second year averages across those two years; there’s no requirement to invent a third year’s figure or wait until year three to start complying, if the thresholds are otherwise crossed.

A smaller obligation still means a smaller committee, not no committee

One genuine relief provision: if a company’s CSR obligation for the year works out to ₹50 lakh or less, it isn’t required to constitute a full, separate CSR Committee. The Board itself can discharge the committee’s functions directly. This doesn’t remove the company from CSR altogether, the 2% obligation and the reporting requirements still apply, it just removes one governance layer for companies whose obligation is genuinely small.

What’s actually in motion right now

There’s real amendment activity around these thresholds in Parliament, and it’s worth knowing about even though nothing has been passed and notified as this is written. Different proposals in circulation point in different directions, some describe raising the net-profit threshold, which would narrow the pool of companies covered, while others describe lowering the net worth and turnover thresholds substantially, which would expand it to catch many more mid-sized companies. Given that the proposals on the table don’t even agree on direction, the only responsible thing to do with this section is flag it as unsettled rather than predict an outcome. If your company is close to any of the current thresholds, this is worth checking against live MCA notifications before you lock next year’s budget, not something to plan around based on any single article, including this one.

Where this fits into the bigger picture

Applicability is the first gate, but crossing it just tells you whether Section 135 applies at all. What you actually owe, and how that number is calculated, is a separate question.

title: How to Calculate Your Company's 2% CSR Obligation
excerpt: Why your P&L profit isn't the number you need, and a full worked example of the Section 198 calculation.
content:
Your CSR obligation is 2% of average net profit over the three immediately preceding financial years, and that net profit figure is computed under Section 198 of the Companies Act, not lifted directly from your profit and loss statement. The two numbers are often close, but they’re rarely identical, and the gap between them is where most calculation errors happen.

Why your P&L profit isn’t the number you need

Section 198 was written for a different original purpose, capping managerial remuneration, and CSR calculation was later required to use the same adjusted figure, under Rule 2(h) of the CSR Policy Rules. That figure strips out anything that looks like a one-off capital event and adds back a few items your P&L may have already deducted. The result is a number that’s meant to reflect the company’s steady operating performance, not whatever happened to hit the books that particular year.

Using your P&L’s bottom line instead, or worse, your Income Tax Act taxable income, is the single most common calculation mistake companies make on this obligation. It’s an understandable shortcut, the audited P&L is right there and easy to reach for, but it produces the wrong number in either direction depending on what happened that year.

What gets excluded from the Section 198 figure

A handful of items don’t count as profit at all for this calculation, even though they might appear as profit in your P&L:

  • Capital gains, including profit from selling an entire undertaking or part of one
  • Profit from selling immovable property or fixed assets of a capital nature, unless the company’s actual business is buying and selling that kind of asset
  • Any profit made on the premium at which the company issued its own shares or debentures
  • Profits earned by overseas branches
  • Unrealised or notional gains, including revaluation-driven changes in the carrying value of an asset or liability that haven’t actually been realized

What has to be added back

On the other side, a few deductions your P&L already took have to be added back before you arrive at the Section 198 figure, because Section 198 doesn’t treat them as legitimate reductions to operating profit:

  • Income tax
  • Compensation, damages, or payments of a capital nature
  • Capital losses

Depreciation is treated normally and doesn’t need to be added back, it’s allowed as a standard deduction at the rates specified in the Act. Government subsidies received by the company are generally excluded from the profit figure too, unless the Central Government has specifically directed otherwise for that subsidy, so a year with a large government grant baked into the P&L needs the same careful unpacking as a year with a one-off capital gain.

What if one of the three years was a loss

This comes up more often than companies expect, and the treatment isn’t always intuitive. If the Section 198 computation produces a loss in one of the three preceding years, that year still enters the average as a negative figure rather than being excluded or treated as zero. A company with adjusted net profits of ₹18 crore, a loss of ₹3 crore, and ₹25 crore across three years averages to ₹13.33 crore, not an average of the two profitable years alone. Leaving the loss year out of the calculation entirely, treating it as if it didn’t happen, is a mistake that inflates the obligation and creates its own problem: a company can end up budgeting for, and spending, more than the law actually requires, which isn’t itself a violation, but is worth catching before it happens rather than after.

If the three-year average itself works out to a loss, the company has no CSR obligation for that year at all. There’s nothing to spend 2% of when the base figure is negative.

A worked example

Take a mid-sized logistics company with the following profit-before-tax figures across three years: ₹22 crore, ₹28 crore, and ₹31 crore. In the most recent year, the P&L also included a one-off ₹4 crore capital gain from selling a warehouse the company doesn’t otherwise trade in, and the company paid ₹6 crore in income tax that year, already deducted in arriving at that ₹31 crore figure.

Working through the adjustment: the ₹4 crore capital gain gets excluded (it’s a capital-nature item, not operating profit), and the ₹6 crore income tax gets added back (Section 198 doesn’t allow it as a deduction). That most recent year’s adjusted net profit becomes ₹31 crore minus ₹4 crore plus ₹6 crore, or ₹33 crore, a meaningfully different number from the ₹31 crore the P&L shows.

Averaging the three adjusted years, assuming the first two years needed no material adjustment, gives ₹27.67 crore, and the CSR obligation for the coming year is 2% of that: about ₹55.3 lakh. Anyone who calculated this straight off the unadjusted P&L figures would have landed on a noticeably different, and lower, obligation, one that wouldn’t hold up if the calculation were ever reviewed.

A common myth worth correcting directly

A question that comes up constantly: does this year’s CSR expenditure need to be added back when calculating next year’s obligation, since it reduced this year’s P&L profit? The answer is no. CSR spend is not an item Section 198 requires you to add back, and treating it as one would understate future obligations for the wrong reason. The confusion usually comes from mixing up the CSR calculation with the separate managerial remuneration calculation, which draws on the same Section 198 base figure but has its own distinct set of adjustments.

For companies that haven’t completed three financial years yet

If your company has only one or two completed financial years behind it, the average is calculated across whichever years actually exist, not backfilled with an assumed figure for the missing year. A company in its second year averages across those two years alone. This is covered in more depth, alongside the full applicability picture, in the companion article on Section 135 applicability.

A practical checklist before you finalize the number

  • Start from PBT per the audited P&L, not the reported net profit after tax, and not taxable income under the Income Tax Act.
  • Exclude any capital-nature gains, share or debenture premium income, and overseas branch profit.
  • Add back income tax, capital losses, and capital-nature compensation or damages.
  • Leave depreciation as-is, don’t add it back.
  • Confirm the calculation is done standalone, on this company’s own financials, not the group’s consolidated numbers.
  • Get the final figure signed off by whoever certifies your CSR-2 filing before you build a budget around it, not after.

That last step matters more than it might seem. A budget built on an uncertified number is a budget that might need to be revised mid-year, which is a harder conversation to have with a CSR Committee than getting the figure right the first time.

title: Choosing a CSR Implementing Partner: What CSR-1 Registration Actually Means
excerpt: What CSR-1 registration actually certifies, and the questions worth asking beyond it.
content:
CSR-1 registration is a mandatory MCA filing that every implementing agency has needed since April 2021 to legally receive CSR funds. It confirms the entity is a real, eligible, income-tax-registered organization with a track record. It does not tell you whether that organization will actually be a good partner to work with, and treating it as the whole due-diligence process is where most partner-selection mistakes start.

What CSR-1 registration actually certifies

To register, an organization has to be one of a defined set of entity types: a Section 8 company, a registered public trust, a registered society, or an entity established under an Act of Parliament or a State legislature, or by the Central or State government. It also has to already hold valid registration under Section 12A (now 12AB) and Section 80G of the Income Tax Act before it can even file CSR-1, that’s a precondition, not a parallel check you do separately. Beyond that, most eligibility routes require a minimum three-year track record of relevant activity, with an exception for entities the funding company itself helped establish.

Once filed, correctly signed by the entity’s director, trustee, or chairperson depending on its structure, and certified by a practicing Chartered Accountant, Company Secretary, or Cost Accountant, the MCA portal issues a unique CSR Registration Number automatically, along with a digitally signed approval letter. No government fee applies to the filing itself.

What that number actually certifies is narrow: this organization exists, is the right kind of legal entity, and is tax-registered. It says nothing about whether the organization is well run, financially sound beyond the basics, or good at the specific kind of work you’re funding.

What CSR-1 doesn’t tell you

Registration is a floor, not a recommendation. Two organizations can both hold valid CSR-1 numbers and be wildly different partners to actually work with, one with strong program delivery and transparent reporting, the other barely functional beyond the paperwork that got it registered in the first place. The number confirms eligibility to receive funds, not competence at deploying them well.

This matters because it’s tempting, especially under time pressure to finalize a year’s CSR spend, to treat “do they have a CSR Registration Number” as the only question worth asking. It’s a necessary question. It isn’t a sufficient one.

What goes wrong if you skip the check

Routing funds through an organization that turns out not to be CSR-1 registered, or whose 12A/80G status had quietly lapsed before the transfer, doesn’t just create a paperwork problem to sort out later. The expenditure gets disqualified from counting as CSR spend at all, regardless of what the money actually accomplished on the ground. A company can fund a genuinely well-run project, see real outcomes, and still end up with an unspent obligation on its books because the receiving organization’s registration wasn’t in order. The verification step isn’t bureaucratic caution for its own sake, it’s the difference between spend that counts and spend that doesn’t.

One related restriction worth knowing if you’re considering an international organization or foreign foundation as part of your CSR delivery: they generally can’t act as the implementing agency actually receiving and deploying funds. They can be brought in for specific supporting roles, designing a project, monitoring and evaluating it, or building capacity among your own CSR team, but the entity holding and spending the money has to be a CSR-1 registered Indian organization.

How to actually verify it

Don’t take an organization’s word, or even a certificate they hand you, for their registration status. The MCA portal lets you look up a CSR Registration Number independently, and that direct check should happen before funds move, not after. The same goes for 12A/80G status: those registrations can lapse or be revoked without CSR-1 registration itself formally expiring, since CSR-1 is broadly a one-time registration that doesn’t require periodic renewal on its own. An organization’s underlying tax registrations staying current is on them to maintain, and on you to periodically re-check, not something you verify once and assume holds forever.

There’s been a real tightening here recently too: more recent guidance has pushed registering entities toward more specific disclosure, naming exactly which eligibility route they’re relying on rather than a general assertion, and disclosing more detail about governing body members. If you’re evaluating a partner that registered years ago under looser disclosure norms, it’s worth asking them to confirm their registration still reflects current standards, rather than assuming an old approval letter tells the whole story.

What actually makes a partnership work, beyond the paperwork

In practice: registration answers “can we legally fund them.” It doesn’t answer “will this actually be a good day for the people it’s meant to reach.” When Team Up joined Giving Tree Foundation and Way of Hope Charitable Trust’s Independence Day Children’s Festival, the useful clarity wasn’t about registration status at all, it was about role. The festival’s organizers ran the day; Team Up joined as a participant, the same way any funding partner should show up, rather than trying to direct an event that wasn’t theirs to direct. That kind of clarity, who’s actually running the show and who’s supporting it, tends to predict a smoother partnership far better than a registration number does.

Questions worth asking beyond CSR-1 and 12A/80G status: How long has this organization actually run programs like the one you’re funding, not just how long has it existed. Who else has funded them, and would those funders talk to you about the experience. What does their reporting actually look like after a project closes, not just before it starts. Registration tells you they’re allowed to receive the money. These questions tell you whether they’ll use it well.

A short due-diligence checklist

  • Confirm the CSR Registration Number independently on the MCA portal, don’t rely solely on a certificate provided by the organization.
  • Verify 12A/80G status is current, separately from CSR-1 status, since one can lapse without affecting the other.
  • Ask for specific examples of past project delivery and reporting, not just a general capability statement.
  • Talk to at least one other funder or partner who’s worked with them before, if you can.
  • Get clarity in writing on who’s responsible for what on the day itself, this heads off more friction than any registration check will.
  • Set a re-check cadence, even a simple annual one, for multi-year partnerships, rather than treating the upfront check as good for the life of the relationship.

Passing this checklist doesn’t guarantee a great partnership. Skipping it makes a bad one much more likely, and for a multi-year commitment, the check that mattered at signing can quietly stop being true two years in without anyone noticing until an audit asks.

title: What Happens to Unspent CSR Funds
excerpt: The two paths an unspent CSR amount can take, and what a missed transfer deadline actually costs.
content:
Underspending your CSR obligation isn’t itself illegal. Leaving the shortfall unaddressed is. Once you know a gap exists, the unspent amount has to move to one of two places within a strict deadline, depending on whether it was earmarked for an ongoing project, and missing that transfer deadline carries its own separate penalty, even when the underlying spending itself was handled correctly.

Why it matters which path applies

Everything here turns on one categorization decision the Board has to make and document: was the unspent amount tied to an ongoing, Board-approved multi-year project, or not. Get that categorization right, and the deadlines and mechanics below are straightforward. Get it wrong, treating an informal continuation of activities as if it were a properly approved ongoing project, and you can end up defaulting on a deadline you didn’t realize applied to you.

Path one: unspent funds tied to an ongoing project

If the shortfall relates to a Board-approved ongoing project, the company opens a dedicated Unspent CSR Account at a scheduled bank and transfers the unspent amount into it within 30 days of the financial year’s end, by April 30 for a March 31 year-end. That account gets disclosed as a current liability on the balance sheet, not tucked away as a footnote.

The money then has to actually be spent, in line with the CSR policy, within the following three financial years. An “ongoing project” itself has a ceiling: it can run for a maximum of four years including its year of approval, or three years counted from the year after commencement, depending on which framing you use. A project running longer than that stops qualifying as ongoing and needs to be restructured or formally closed.

If, after those three years, some balance is still unspent, it doesn’t sit there indefinitely. It has to be transferred, within 30 days of the end of that third financial year, to a fund specified under Schedule VII.

Path two: unspent funds not tied to any project

If the shortfall isn’t tied to an ongoing project at all, there’s no intermediate account. The unspent amount goes directly to a Schedule VII fund within six months of the financial year’s end, by September 30 for a March 31 year-end. Eligible funds include the Prime Minister’s National Relief Fund, the PM CARES Fund, the Clean Ganga Fund, and any other fund the Central Government specifically notifies for this purpose. It’s not a company’s choice to invent its own recipient; the destination has to be one of these designated funds.

A worked example

Take a company with a calculated CSR obligation of ₹20 lakh for the year, based on the standard three-year average. Through the year, it actually spends ₹8 lakh, leaving ₹12 lakh unspent. Of that ₹12 lakh, ₹5 lakh was earmarked for a Board-approved two-year education project already underway, and the remaining ₹7 lakh had no such project attached, it was simply general obligation that didn’t get deployed.

The ₹5 lakh follows the ongoing-project path: into the Unspent CSR Account within 30 days of the financial year’s end, to be spent over the project’s remaining approved timeline. The ₹7 lakh follows the non-ongoing path: transferred directly to a Schedule VII fund within six months. Two different amounts, two different destinations, two different clocks, all triggered by the same underspend.

What happens if you miss the deadline

The penalty structure is identical for both paths, and it’s calibrated to the amount that should have been transferred, not the company’s total CSR obligation for the year. The company faces a penalty of twice the amount required to be transferred, or ₹1 crore, whichever is lower. Every officer in default faces a personal penalty of one-tenth of that amount, or ₹2 lakh, whichever is lower.

This isn’t a theoretical risk. In one adjudication handled by the Registrar of Companies, Delhi, a company that owed roughly ₹10.24 lakh in a Schedule VII transfer for FY 2022-23 missed its September 30, 2023 deadline and didn’t complete the transfer until March 2025, more than a year late. The company had, by its own admission, simply let the deadline pass. Penalties were imposed on the company and on the directors who remained in office through the default period; two directors who had left before the deadline were found not liable, since the obligation attaches to whoever was actually responsible for compliance at the time. The underlying point holds regardless of the exact figures in any one case: a late transfer is treated as a live violation for as long as it stays unresolved, not a paperwork delay that gets forgiven once the money eventually moves.

The disclosure obligation doesn’t end at the transfer

Moving the money on time isn’t the last step. The Board still has to specify, in the company’s annual report, the reasons the amount went unspent in the first place, and this requirement doesn’t disappear once the transfer is complete. A company that transferred its unspent amount perfectly on schedule but skipped the reasoning in its Board Report has still left part of the obligation undone. The disclosure exists so that anyone reading the report, a regulator, an auditor, a shareholder, can see not just that money moved, but why it didn’t get spent as originally planned, and whether that reason suggests a one-off issue or a pattern worth watching in future years.

Where companies actually go wrong

A few patterns show up repeatedly in default cases:

  • Not opening the Unspent CSR Account within the 30-day window, sometimes because nobody was tracking the deadline against the financial year close rather than the AGM date.
  • Treating an informal continuation of last year’s activities as an “ongoing project” without the Board approval and documentation that classification actually requires.
  • Missing an Annual Action Plan altogether, which is meant to set out the year’s CSR spend in advance and makes the ongoing-versus-non-ongoing categorization much easier to get right from the start.

Staying ahead of it

The practical fix is mostly a calendar problem, not a legal one: know your financial year end, mark April 30 and September 30 as hard dates regardless of when your AGM happens to fall, and get the Board’s categorization of ongoing versus non-ongoing spend documented before the financial year closes, not scrambled together afterward. Companies that default on these deadlines are rarely doing so because the rule was unclear. They’re doing so because nobody owned the date.

(Next: CSR Reporting and Filing: CSR-2, the Board Report, and What Gets Checked.)

title: CSR Reporting and Filing: CSR-2, the Board Report, and What Gets Checked
excerpt: CSR-2, the Board Report's own annexure, and a deadline that's messier in practice than the rule suggests.
content:
CSR compliance doesn’t end when the money moves. Every company under Section 135 has to file a detailed Form CSR-2 covering spend and project data, annex CSR disclosures to its Board Report, and publish its CSR policy on its website. Listed companies carry an additional layer on top, BRSR filings under SEBI. The mechanics of when and how CSR-2 actually gets filed have also genuinely shifted more than once in recent years, which is worth knowing before you plan a filing calendar around it.

What gets filed, and where

Three separate disclosures make up a company’s CSR reporting obligation, and they don’t all live in the same document:

  • Form CSR-2, an eleven-page form covering CSR amount spent across the preceding financial years and details of every ongoing and completed project, filed with the Registrar of Companies.
  • The Board Report’s CSR annexure, covering the CSR policy, the CSR Committee’s composition, the calculated obligation, actual spend, and the reasons for any shortfall.
  • The CSR policy itself, published on the company’s website, freely accessible rather than buried in a filing only regulators see.

Getting one of these right doesn’t cover the other two. Companies sometimes treat CSR-2 as the whole obligation because it’s the most detailed of the three, but a company that files a flawless CSR-2 and forgets to keep its CSR policy current on its website is still out of compliance.

Form CSR-2: what it actually covers

CSR-2 asks for the CSR obligation amount, the actual amount spent, and a project-by-project breakdown, activity, location, spend, and the implementing agency’s CSR Registration Number for each. It also covers the status of any ongoing projects and details of amounts sitting in the Unspent CSR Account, alongside an impact assessment summary where one was required. Only Board-approved CSR activities that were actually completed during the financial year get reported here; money that was planned or reserved but not yet spent doesn’t belong in this year’s figures, it belongs in next year’s, or in the unspent-funds disclosure instead.

The form has to be digitally signed by the Company Secretary and a director, and certified by a practicing Chartered Accountant, a layer of independent sign-off that’s meant to catch inconsistencies before the filing goes in, not after.

The deadline is messier in practice than the rule suggests

The rule on paper says CSR-2 is filed as an addendum to Form AOC-4, within 30 days of the AGM, the same clock as your financial statements. In practice, that hasn’t quite been how it’s worked. The technical capability to file CSR-2 as a true linked addendum to AOC-4 still hasn’t been built into the MCA’s filing system, so companies file it as a separate standalone form after AOC-4 goes through, and the MCA has issued a fresh, specific deadline for CSR-2 nearly every year rather than letting the general 30-day rule simply apply. FY 2021-22’s CSR-2 got a standalone deadline of March 31, 2023. FY 2022-23 got March 31, 2024. FY 2023-24’s deadline was set, then pushed to December 31, 2024, then extended again to June 30, 2025.

The practical takeaway isn’t that the deadline is lax, it’s that you shouldn’t assume the “30 days after AGM” rule tells you the actual date. Check the current year’s specific MCA notification before you build a filing calendar, rather than working backward from your AGM date and assuming that’s the deadline. As of recent guidance, there’s also no separate statutory penalty specifically written for late CSR-2 filing the way there is for the unspent-fund transfer deadlines, though that’s worth reconfirming against current rules each year rather than treated as a permanent feature, and a company with an otherwise messy compliance record won’t find “no specific penalty” much comfort if it draws wider regulatory attention.

What actually gets checked

Company law professionals have flagged a recurring issue worth knowing about directly: CSR figures reported in a company’s financial statements, filed through AOC-4, sometimes don’t match the figures reported separately in CSR-2. That mismatch is exactly the kind of thing that draws a second look, and it’s part of why the MCA has moved toward requiring companies to keep AOC-4 and CSR-2 records genuinely distinct and reconciled with each other, rather than treating CSR-2 as an afterthought filled in loosely once the main financial statements are already locked.

The practical fix is straightforward: whoever prepares CSR-2 should be working from the same underlying numbers as whoever prepared the CSR figures in the financial statements, not reconstructing them independently from memory or a separate spreadsheet.

What you actually need on hand before filing

Beyond the raw spend figures, a smooth CSR-2 filing typically needs project reports covering each project’s objectives, outcomes, and supporting evidence, completion certificates, photographs, whatever documents that project’s own governance produced, plus a clear record of any amounts sitting in the Unspent CSR Account or transferred to Schedule VII funds during the year. Assembling this after the fact, once the filing deadline is already close, is where most of the last-minute scramble comes from. Companies that keep this documentation current project by project, through the year rather than at year-end, tend to find the actual filing itself is the easy part.

The Board Report’s own CSR annexure

Separately from CSR-2, the Board’s Report to shareholders needs its own annexure covering the CSR policy, the CSR Committee’s composition, the average net profit calculation, the prescribed and actual spend, and, where relevant, the same reasons-for-shortfall disclosure covered in the unspent-funds article. This has to be signed by the chairperson of the CSR Committee, or a director the Board specifically authorizes, and it forms part of the same annual filing package that goes to the Registrar of Companies alongside the financial statements.

Listed companies: one more layer

If your company is listed, CSR reporting doesn’t stop at Section 135’s requirements. SEBI’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting framework, BRSR, requires its own disclosures on environmental, social, and governance performance, and CSR activity typically features prominently in the social section. BRSR and CSR-2 cover overlapping ground but aren’t the same filing and don’t substitute for each other; a listed company still owes both.

Keeping this manageable

The companies that handle CSR reporting smoothly tend to do the same few things: they check the current year’s specific CSR-2 deadline rather than assuming last year’s date still applies, they keep one shared source of CSR spend figures that both the financial statements and CSR-2 draw from, and they get the Board’s CSR annexure drafted alongside the rest of the annual report rather than as a late addition once everything else is finalized. None of this is complicated. It’s mostly a matter of not treating three separate disclosures as if they’re really just one.

(Next: Employee Engagement vs. Compliance-Only CSR: What Actually Moves the Needle.)

title: Employee Engagement vs. Compliance-Only CSR: What Actually Moves the Needle
excerpt: What the research actually says about which kind of CSR moves employee engagement, and which metrics most programs get wrong.
content:
Spending your 2% obligation satisfies the law. It doesn’t automatically satisfy the employees who show up to whatever the money funded. Research on corporate volunteering and CSR participation points to a specific, testable gap: most programs measure activity, hours logged, headcount attending, rather than outcomes, actual engagement or retention effects, and the data on what genuinely predicts engagement looks different from what most CSR budgets are quietly optimized for.

The metric most programs actually track, and why it’s the wrong one

Participation rate and volunteer hours are the numbers almost every CSR program reports, and for good reason: they’re easy to collect and simple to put in a slide. But as the volunteering-technology firm Goodera’s 2026 industry report on volunteering trends puts it plainly, a company that logs 10,000 volunteer hours across 500 employees has demonstrated activity. It hasn’t demonstrated impact. Without outcome measurement sitting alongside the hours logged, a CSR program ends up competing for budget on optics rather than evidence, no different from any other line item nobody can prove is working.

The report’s own recommendation is a shift toward measuring what actually changed: employee engagement scores, retention data, and skill development, correlated against who participated and how, not just how many hours got logged in a spreadsheet.

What’s actually happening to participation, and it’s not what you’d expect

A large-scale longitudinal study by Benevity, tracking over ten million users across more than 400 companies, found something worth sitting with: average program participation rates have been rising, up roughly 30% over recent years. At the same time, the depth of that participation has been falling, average hours per volunteer dropped from 16.4 to 12.7 per year over a six-year period. More people are showing up. Each of them is doing less, on average, when they do.

Read together, that’s not a contradiction, it’s a trend line: employee volunteering is moving away from ongoing-commitment models and toward episodic, event-based participation. More people will show up once, for something specific and well-defined, than will sign up for an open-ended ongoing commitment. In India specifically, Goodera’s data on corporate volunteering programs found a median workforce participation rate of 32%, with in-person activity accounting for 84% of volunteering events, a strong signal that Indian employees specifically favor hands-on, present, one-time participation over more abstract or remote forms of involvement.

Which kind of CSR actually engages employees

A separate, India-specific academic study on employee volunteerism and engagement found a strong positive relationship between CSR participation and employee engagement overall, with one detail worth calling out directly: CSR activity oriented toward society, the actual community-facing work, had a stronger relationship with engagement than CSR framed around internal employee benefit. The same study identified emotional engagement as the most influential variable in the relationship between CSR participation and employee commitment, ahead of more procedural or transactional factors.

Put plainly: the CSR that moves employees isn’t the CSR that’s about them. It’s the CSR that puts them inside something real, happening to real people, where what they feel in the moment is the thing actually driving the retention and commitment effect researchers are able to measure afterward.

There’s a genuine caveat worth stating directly rather than glossing over: these are correlational findings, not controlled experiments. A study showing that community-facing CSR correlates more strongly with engagement than employee-facing CSR doesn’t prove one causes the other; companies that invest more thoughtfully in community-facing programs may simply also invest more thoughtfully everywhere else. The data is still useful for deciding where to look harder, but it’s not a guarantee, and treating it as an iron law would be overstating what the research actually shows. A separate, often-cited figure worth including for balance: 92% of business leaders surveyed by Deloitte agree that volunteering improves employees’ professional skills, a benefit that sits alongside engagement rather than instead of it, and one that doesn’t depend on the community-facing versus employee-facing distinction at all.

What this means for how a CSR day actually gets designed

None of this argues against compliance-first thinking, the 2% has to be spent correctly regardless. It argues for a specific design question sitting alongside the compliance one: given that episodic, in-person, emotionally real participation is what the data associates with actual engagement, is the day itself built to be memorable, or just built to be compliant?

Those aren’t automatically the same day. A CSR activity can satisfy every Schedule VII requirement, get filed correctly in CSR-2, and still be forgettable to the employees who attended it, nothing about compliance guarantees the emotional weight the research keeps pointing to as the actual driver. Building that in is a separate decision, made deliberately, on top of the spend the law already requires, not a byproduct of getting the paperwork right.

The measurement gap, in practice

Beyond the post-event survey, the metrics that outcome-focused research keeps pointing back to are worth naming specifically, since “measure outcomes, not just activity” is easy to agree with and hard to actually operationalize without a starting list:

  • Post-event sentiment, a short, simple survey immediately after, not months later when memory has faded.
  • Repeat participation rate, whether the same employees choose to show up again, a stronger signal than first-time attendance alone.
  • Correlation with HR engagement data, if your company already runs periodic engagement surveys, checking whether CSR participants score differently is a low-effort way to start connecting the two datasets that usually sit in separate departments.

None of these require new software or a large budget. They require deciding, before the next event, that hours logged and headcount attending aren’t the whole story, and building the small additional step that captures what they miss.

There’s also a seasonal pattern worth knowing for planning purposes: Goodera’s data on Indian corporate volunteering shows Q4 consistently drawing the highest participation, averaging around 50 volunteers per event, well above other quarters. If episodic, well-designed single events are genuinely where engagement comes from, when you schedule them matters as much as how you design them, and a CSR calendar built around Q4 as an afterthought is working against a pattern the data already shows.

title: CSR Compliance FAQ: Quick Answers to the Questions CSR Teams Ask Most
excerpt: Twenty fast, standalone answers to the CSR compliance questions that come up most often.
content:
Fast, standalone answers to the questions that come up most often around CSR compliance in India. Each answer stands on its own, no need to read the others first.

Is CSR mandatory in India? Yes. Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, companies crossing a set net worth, turnover, or net profit threshold in the preceding financial year are legally required to spend at least 2% of average net profit on CSR, form a CSR Committee, and report their spending. India was the first country to make CSR a statutory obligation rather than a voluntary choice, and non-compliance carries defined financial penalties for both the company and its officers.

What’s the minimum CSR spending requirement? Companies covered under Section 135 must spend at least 2% of their average net profit, calculated under Section 198 of the Companies Act, across the three financial years immediately preceding the current one. This is a floor, not a fixed target. Companies are free to spend more, and many do, but 2% is the legally mandated minimum before penalties for underspending apply.

Which companies must comply with Section 135? Any company registered in India, public, private, or Section 8, or a foreign company with an Indian branch or project office, that crosses any one of three thresholds in the preceding financial year: net worth above ₹500 crore, turnover above ₹1,000 crore, or net profit above ₹5 crore. Only one threshold needs to be crossed, and applicability is reassessed fresh every year based on that year’s figures alone.

How is the CSR 2% actually calculated? Take the company’s Section 198 net profit, not the profit and loss statement figure or taxable income, across each of the three immediately preceding financial years, average the three, and multiply by 2%. Section 198 excludes capital-nature gains and overseas branch profit, and adds back items like income tax and capital losses, so the result often differs from the number on the audited P&L.

What is Form CSR-1? Form CSR-1 is the mandatory registration an implementing agency, an NGO, trust, or Section 8 company, files with the MCA to legally receive CSR funds. Filing requires the organization already hold valid 12A and 80G registration under the Income Tax Act, plus typically a three-year track record. Once approved, a unique CSR Registration Number is issued; routing funds through an unregistered entity gets that spend disqualified as CSR expenditure entirely.

What is Form CSR-2, and when is it filed? Form CSR-2 is the detailed annual report companies file with the Registrar of Companies, covering CSR obligation, actual spend, project-by-project detail, and unspent fund status. It’s meant to be filed as an addendum to Form AOC-4, but in practice the MCA has issued a separate, standalone deadline nearly every year rather than a fixed 30-days-after-AGM rule, so the current year’s specific notification should always be checked directly.

Can unspent CSR funds carry forward? Yes, but only for amounts tied to a Board-approved ongoing project. That amount moves into a dedicated Unspent CSR Account within 30 days of the financial year’s end and has to be spent within the following three years. Unspent amounts with no ongoing project attached don’t carry forward at all; they’re transferred directly to a Schedule VII fund within six months instead.

What happens if a company underspends its CSR obligation? Underspending itself isn’t illegal, but leaving the gap unaddressed is. The company has to disclose the reasons for the shortfall in its Board Report and transfer the unspent amount, either into an Unspent CSR Account for an ongoing project or directly to a Schedule VII fund if there’s no ongoing project, within a strict deadline. Missing that transfer deadline triggers its own separate financial penalty.

What is the Unspent CSR Account? A dedicated account at a scheduled bank that holds CSR funds earmarked for a Board-approved ongoing project but not yet spent by the financial year’s end. Companies must open it and transfer the unspent amount within 30 days of the year closing, disclose it as a current liability on the balance sheet, and spend the balance within three years, or transfer whatever remains to a Schedule VII fund.

What are the penalties for CSR non-compliance? For failing to transfer unspent CSR funds within the required deadline, the company faces a penalty of twice the amount that should have been transferred, or ₹1 crore, whichever is lower. Every officer in default faces a personal penalty of one-tenth of that amount, or ₹2 lakh, whichever is lower. These penalties attach to the missed transfer specifically, not the company’s full-year CSR obligation.

Can a company run CSR activities directly, without a partner? Yes. Companies aren’t required to route CSR funds through an external implementing agency; they can design and deliver CSR activities themselves, provided the activities fall within Schedule VII and are properly documented and reported. Many companies use a mix of direct delivery and registered implementing partners, depending on the project and the internal capacity available to run it.

What is Schedule VII? Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013 is the defined list of activity categories eligible to count as CSR spend, covering areas including education, healthcare, poverty relief, environmental sustainability, gender equality, disaster relief, and heritage protection, among others. A company’s CSR policy has to map its planned activities to this list, and the Board is responsible for confirming that mapping before any spend happens.

Does employee volunteering time count as CSR spend? No. Volunteer hours can’t be monetized and counted toward the 2% obligation, regardless of how many employees participate or how valuable their time was. What can count is a project that’s already CSR-eligible on its own merits, funded through the actual CSR budget, with employees participating alongside that spend. Volunteering adds engagement value on top of the spend; it isn’t a substitute for it.

Is CSR impact assessment mandatory? Only for companies meeting both of two conditions: an average CSR obligation of ₹10 crore or more across the preceding three financial years, and a specific project with an outlay of ₹1 crore or more that’s been completed at least a year before the assessment begins. Where required, the assessment has to be done by an independent third-party agency, with costs capped at 5% of CSR spend or ₹50 lakh, whichever is lower.

Can CSR funds be pooled across group companies? CSR applicability and the 2% calculation are assessed on a standalone basis, one company at a time, not on a consolidated group basis. A holding company being covered doesn’t automatically pull in its subsidiaries, and vice versa. Group companies can collaborate on shared CSR projects, but each entity’s own obligation is calculated and met independently, based on its own financials, not pooled across the group.

Who must sit on a company’s CSR Committee? At least three directors, with a minimum of one independent director, for most companies. Companies not required to appoint an independent director under the Act can constitute a smaller, two-director committee instead. Foreign companies covered under Section 135 use a different structure: two people, one an India resident authorized to accept notices on the company’s behalf, the other nominated by the foreign company itself.

Do private companies have to comply? Yes. Section 135 applies to every company that crosses the applicability thresholds, and that includes private limited companies, not just publicly listed ones. Section 8 companies, the not-for-profit structure under the Act, are covered the same way too. Company type doesn’t create an exemption; only falling below all three financial thresholds does.

Is CSR spend tax-deductible? No. CSR expenditure cannot be claimed as a business expense for income tax purposes, a position confirmed since the Finance Act, 2014. This is separate from the deductions donors can claim under Section 80G for contributions made directly to an eligible registered organization outside the CSR framework, which follow entirely different rules.

What’s the deadline for filing CSR-2? Nominally 30 days after the AGM, as an addendum to Form AOC-4. In practice, the MCA has issued a distinct standalone deadline for CSR-2 nearly every year since it was introduced, often with extensions, rather than letting the general rule apply automatically. The safest approach is checking the current year’s specific MCA notification directly rather than assuming the AGM-plus-30-days rule is the operative date.

Is the 2% threshold changing in 2026? Possibly, but nothing has been passed and notified as of this writing. Different amendment proposals are in circulation, some describing a higher net-profit threshold that would narrow the pool of companies covered, others describing lower net worth and turnover thresholds that would expand it. Since the proposals don’t even agree on direction, this is worth checking against live MCA notifications before assuming any specific change, rather than relying on any single source, including this one.
